question: Tell me about a time when you enabled your team/a team member to implement a significant change or improvement. What problem were you trying to solve? How did you measure success? What was the end result/impact?

raiseTranscript.text: Our on-call rotation had a manual checklist that took 20 minutes per handoff. I noticed a teammate was duplicating steps in a spreadsheet, so I wrote a short internal wiki page and a simple Python wrapper that auto-pulled the last 24h metrics.
What exactly did the teammate do after you shared it?
She took the wiki page, added two more fields we had missed, and rolled it out to the whole rotation. We tracked handoff time in a shared doc for two weeks.
What were the numbers?
Average handoff dropped from 20 min to 7 min. The team did 12 handoffs that month so roughly 2.5 hours saved.

raiseNotes: Q: enabled team member to implement change
Situation: manual 20-min handoff checklist
Action: wrote wiki + Python wrapper, teammate extended it
Outcome: 20min -> 7min, ~2.5h saved/month
Quote: "She took the wiki page, added two more fields"
Follow-up: metrics tracked in shared doc for two weeks
junior.raiseFeedback: Raises the bar for Invent and Simplify at junior level. The candidate identified a repetitive local process, created a lightweight artifact, and handed ownership to a teammate who then improved it further. Concrete before/after numbers (20 min to 7 min) show the simplification had measurable effect even at individual scope. The story stays within expected junior boundaries while demonstrating coachability and willingness to let someone else finish the work. Main gap is lack of any cross-team ripple, which is acceptable at this level.

lowerTranscript.text: I refactored a function that was getting slow.
How did you enable anyone else?
I showed the PR to my teammate and they merged it.
What problem were you solving and how did you measure it?
It was just slow. I didn't track anything after the merge.

lowerNotes: Q: enabled team member to implement change
Situation: vague "slow function"
Action: wrote PR, showed to teammate
Outcome: teammate merged it, no metrics
Quote: "I didn't track anything after the merge"
Follow-up: no before/after data or ownership transfer
junior.lowerFeedback: Lowers the bar for Invent and Simplify at junior level. The candidate describes a solo refactor with no evidence of enabling anyone else or simplifying a process others could reuse. Absence of any success metric or follow-up measurement shows weak ownership of outcomes. The story never moves beyond "I fixed my code" which does not demonstrate the principle even at the most local scope.

raiseTranscript.text: Two teams were duplicating the same data pipeline for reporting. I created a shared library with a thin abstraction and ran two working sessions so each team could migrate one report.
How did you get both teams to adopt it?
I started with the most painful report, showed a 40% reduction in runtime, then let the other team own the next migration.
What was the final impact?
Four reports moved over three months. Duplicate code dropped from 1,800 lines to under 300. Both teams now contribute fixes back to the library.

raiseNotes: Q: enabled team/a team member to implement change
Situation: duplicate reporting pipelines across two teams
Action: built shared library + ran working sessions
Outcome: 4 reports migrated, 1800 -> 300 LOC, cross-team contributions
Quote: "let the other team own the next migration"
Follow-up: showed 40% runtime win before asking for broader adoption
senior.raiseFeedback: Raises the bar for Invent and Simplify at senior level. The candidate reduced duplication across team boundaries by creating a reusable abstraction and deliberately transferred ownership so others could extend it. Runtime and line-count metrics provide clear evidence of simplification. Influence without authority is visible in the decision to let the second team drive the next migration. Scope and leverage match senior expectations.

lowerTranscript.text: I built a new internal tool that replaced three scripts.
Did any other team adopt it?
Not yet, I was still cleaning it up when I moved to the next project.
How did you measure success?
It felt cleaner to me.

lowerNotes: Q: enabled team to implement change
Situation: replaced three scripts with one tool
Action: built the tool alone
Outcome: no adoption outside own use, no metrics
Quote: "It felt cleaner to me"
Follow-up: project handed off before measuring or driving adoption
senior.lowerFeedback: Lowers the bar for Invent and Simplify at senior level. The candidate produced a local improvement but never enabled other teams or measured impact. Lack of adoption or quantifiable results shows the work stayed at individual scope rather than creating reusable leverage. Senior expectations for cross-team simplification are not met.

raiseTranscript.text: My team was spending 30% of sprint capacity on manual QA for a legacy flow. I asked an engineer to prototype a contract test harness and then had the whole team review and own the rollout.
How did you handle resistance to the new approach?
One senior engineer preferred the old way. I had them run the first pilot so they could see the defect escape rate drop from 12 to 2 per release.
What was the team-level result?
Manual QA time fell to 8% of capacity within two quarters. The same engineer later documented the harness and onboarded two new hires with it.

raiseNotes: Q: enabled team to implement change
Situation: 30% sprint capacity on manual QA
Action: sponsored contract test harness, let team own rollout
Outcome: QA time to 8%, defect escapes 12->2, senior engineer became owner
Quote: "had them run the first pilot"
Follow-up: used data to convert the resister
manager.raiseFeedback: Raises the bar for Invent and Simplify at manager level. The candidate identified a systemic capacity drain, created space for a team-driven solution, and used measurable results to shift behavior. Development of others is clear in the decision to let the resistant senior engineer own the pilot. Team outcome metrics (capacity freed, quality improved) show the manager created leverage rather than performing the work themselves.

lowerTranscript.text: I told the team we needed to automate more tests.
What changed as a result?
A couple people started writing more unit tests but the manual QA load stayed about the same.
Did you track any metrics?
We didn't set a baseline.

lowerNotes: Q: enabled team to implement change
Situation: high manual QA load
Action: told team to automate more
Outcome: no measurable reduction, no baseline
Quote: "We didn't set a baseline"
Follow-up: no ownership transfer or follow-through
manager.lowerFeedback: Lowers the bar for Invent and Simplify at manager level. The candidate issued a direction without creating structure, measurement, or ownership for the improvement. Absence of any baseline or sustained reduction shows the team did not gain new leverage. Manager expectations for developing repeatable team processes are not demonstrated.

raiseTranscript.text: Three product lines were each building their own experimentation platform. I sponsored a single cross-org platform team and required all new experiments to route through it after a six-week pilot.
How did you get the product lines to agree?
I tied platform funding to the shared service and showed the pilot delivered statistically significant results 3x faster than the old per-team approach.
What was the multi-quarter impact?
Within nine months we consolidated three platforms into one, reduced infra spend 35%, and increased experiment velocity by 2.4x across all lines.

raiseNotes: Q: enabled teams to implement change at org scale
Situation: three duplicate experimentation platforms
Action: funded shared platform team, tied funding to adoption
Outcome: 3->1 platform, 35% infra reduction, 2.4x velocity
Quote: "tied platform funding to the shared service"
Follow-up: used pilot data to drive org-wide mandate
exec.raiseFeedback: Raises the bar for Invent and Simplify at exec level. The candidate recognized redundant investment across the organization, created a structural solution (dedicated platform team), and used funding and data to drive adoption. Business-level metrics (infra cost, experiment velocity) demonstrate strategic simplification with lasting leverage. Trade-offs around funding allocation and pilot validation show mature judgment.

lowerTranscript.text: I asked each org to share their experimentation code.
Did duplication decrease?
Some teams looked at each other's repos but kept building separately.
What metrics did you track?
We didn't have a single source of truth for experiment velocity.

lowerNotes: Q: enabled org-level change
Situation: duplicate experimentation efforts
Action: asked teams to share code
Outcome: no consolidation, no velocity metrics
Quote: "kept building separately"
Follow-up: no structural or funding lever applied
exec.lowerFeedback: Lowers the bar for Invent and Simplify at exec level. The candidate relied on voluntary sharing without creating incentives, structure, or measurement. No reduction in duplication or org-level impact was achieved. Executive expectations for strategic simplification and leverage through organizational design are not met.

diagnostic.manager: Own team capacity and ownership transfer
diagnostic.exec: Multiple product lines, platform funding and mandate

diagnostic.junior: Simple time delta with shared doc
diagnostic.senior: Runtime and LOC reduction with adoption data
diagnostic.exec: Infra cost and experiment velocity at org scale

diagnostic.junior: Teammate added fields and rolled out
diagnostic.manager: Resistant engineer became owner and onboarded others
diagnostic.exec: Platform team and product lines sustain the service

diagnostic.manager: Gave pilot ownership to convert resister
diagnostic.exec: Used funding tie and pilot results to mandate adoption
